voiceover.text: So, how do you classify any movement skill? Start with a netball shooter. In training, from one spot, with nobody guarding her, she sinks forty-five shots out of fifty. In matches, from the same spot, she makes about half. Most people say nerves, or tiredness. Both are possible. But there's a third reason, about what kind of task each one is, not how hard it is. And a second puzzle: why would a coach teach a triple jump in parts, but mostly keep a swimming stroke whole?

The syllabus gives four ways to classify a skill, and each one asks a different question. The first asks which muscles do the work. A gross skill uses large muscle groups for force and whole-body coordination, like running or a tackle. A fine skill uses small muscle groups for precision, like a dart throw or a golf putt. Most sport skills are both. Her shot uses her legs and trunk for force, and her fingertips to control the release. So ask which part limits it. When you tire, precision often drops faster than force. So a skill limited by its fine part should sometimes be practised tired, not only fresh.

scenes.title: where does it start and end? continuous, discrete, serial

voiceover.text: The second question is where the movement starts and ends. A continuous skill has no clear start or finish. The end of one cycle is the start of the next, like running or swimming. A discrete skill is one short unit with a clear start and end, like a penalty kick or a free throw. A serial skill is a chain of discrete parts in a fixed order, like a gymnastics routine or a triple jump. This scale decides whether a skill can be broken into parts for practice. Serial skills can. Continuous skills are mostly taught as a whole, because the rhythm is the skill. Kick and pull drills are practice parts, rejoined to the full stroke quickly. That answers the second puzzle. And with a serial skill, practise the joins too, because that's where it fails. A jumper who drills the hop, the step and the jump separately still has to arrive at each phase with the right speed.

scenes.title: how predictable? closed, open, and the shooter

voiceover.text: The third question changes practice the most: how predictable is the environment? A closed skill happens somewhere stable, like a golf putt or a shot put. Nobody interferes, and the goal is one consistent movement, so repeating it under the same conditions is right. An open skill happens somewhere that keeps changing, like passing in a match. Now the skill is reading the situation and choosing a movement, as well as doing it. That reading is called perceptual demand. Back to the shooter. An unguarded shot from one spot is closed. A match shot is open: a defender closing, the pass early, her feet not set. She's trained the doing half, and the reading half has had no practice at all. It's not nerves. It's the drill. But closed practice isn't useless. Earlier, you saw a beginner has no attention to spare, so she starts closed. The mistake is staying there. And a faster or harder closed drill is still closed. Open practice needs a decision made from information she can't know in advance.

scenes.title: who sets the timing? self-paced and externally paced

voiceover.text: The fourth question is who decides when it starts. A self-paced skill starts when the performer chooses, like a free throw. An externally paced skill starts in response to something outside them, like returning a serve, or a sprint start on the gun. These usually line up with closed and open, but they're not the same thing. A sprint start is externally paced, because the gun sets the timing, but it's closed, because the lane never changes. So practise the movement over and over, and practise reacting to an unpredictable gun as a separate job. Pacing also shows where pressure falls. A self-paced skill gives time to prepare, so a routine helps, but nerves have time to build too. An externally paced skill gives no time, so practice trains anticipation against real, varied cues.

Each scale is a line, not two boxes, and the four are independent, so every skill gets four answers. The combination decides the practice. A golf putt is mainly fine, discrete, closed and self-paced, so it suits lots of identical repetitions with a routine. A lay-up in a game uses both muscle types, and it's serial, open and externally paced. So practise the parts, then the joins, then against a real defender, some of it tired. Two skills with a ball and a target, different on three scales, and almost nothing about their practice is the same. And context counts. The same shooting action is closed at the free-throw line and open in play. So a label on its own is half an answer. Say what it changes.
Two things to remember. Classify, then say what it changes. And harder isn't open: open practice needs a decision.

Two exam questions. First. Classify the rowing stroke in a two-thousand-metre race as closed or open, and as continuous, discrete or serial. Then explain one way each classification should shape how it's practised. Pause here to answer.

It's closed, because the water and the lane are stable and nobody interferes. So repeat one consistent stroke many times. And it's continuous, because each stroke runs into the next. So practise it mostly whole, varying rate and distance. The classic mistake is splitting it into parts like a serial skill.

Second. A hockey coach runs a passing drill between two players and fixed cones. To make it more like a game, she doubles the speed and adds a thirty-second countdown. Explain why the drill still won't train passing in a match, and propose one change that would. Pause here to answer.

Passing in a match is open: she has to read defenders and choose a target. The drill is closed, because the partner and the cones never change. Speed and a countdown add pressure, not unpredictability, so the reading half still isn't practised. Add a live defender and two possible receivers, so she must decide every time. The classic mistake is thinking harder means open.

So, for any skill, ask the four questions, then say what each answer changes about practice. Back to the netball shot in a match: open, discrete, and set by the defender's timing. Now you know what kind of task it is. But which practice actually builds it? Why does practice that looks worse work better?
